Q: ASP.NET Web API Publish Fails with Build failed. Check the Output window for more details A:

Can your try the following:

  1. Update publish profile (export from Azure and import into VS the fresh one)

  2. Navigate to your .azurewebsites.net in browser and make sure it doesn’t return 403 Forbidden

  3. Check the diagnostic logs in Azure to see if there is any internal server error

  4. Restart App service and make sure Basic Auth publishing is set to ON under General Settings

  5. Try to use Azure Zip Deployment if nothing works https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/deploy-zip?tabs=cli

Q: How to remove the space between inline/inline-block elements? A:

Unfortunately white-space-collapse is still not implemented.

In the meantime, give the parent element font-size: 0; and set the font-size on the children. This should do the trick

Q: How to cryptographically prove a file existed at a specific time? A:

Many certificate authorities also have an adjacent "Time-Stamping Authority" (TSA) service, where instead of signing a certificate, they sign a provided hash of some arbitrary data. The signature is verifiable using the TSA's certificate chain.

Such timestamping services are commonly used for Authenticode signing (i.e. signing Windows .exe files) – the timestamp service's counter-signature is what prevents a signed .exe from suddenly becoming invalid the next year when the developer's certificate expires. (You can right-click an .exe and go to "Digital Signatures > Details" to see the counter-signature with the CA's timestamp in addition to the signer's self-asserted timestamp.)

For example, DigiCert and Sectigo provide public TSA services, as do Apple1 and Microsoft – all nominally for code-signing purposes but they don't really care what hash you give them. All these services use the RFC 3161 protocol and you can use python-rfc3161 or OpenSSL::Timestamp or openssl ts to generate the requests (to submit via HTTP POST) and/or verify the returned timestamps.

Similar services are also used for eIDAS "qualified document signing" in the XAdES/PAdES/CAdES specifications, where you have a whole set of specifications detailing what kind of auxiliary data (e.g. certificate chains, OCSP responses) must be bundled together with the document to make it fully verifiable offline two decades later.

I don't know if that's common elsewhere in the world, but in my corner of Europe a "digitally-signed contract" would come either as a PAdES-format signed PDF document, or a plain PDF inside XAdES ASiC-E archive, either way with the timestamp and all verification metadata (both for the signer and for the TSA) bundled in the document.

The ¤AdES formats are complex (and the "qualified" timestamping services generally paid-access), but they are a wheel already invented – so if you actually want to timestamp a contract, I'd strongly recommend first looking into whether any such format has already been adopted by law in your region or jurisdiction or whatever.

Keep in mind also that just like there are different lists of "trusted CAs" for different purposes, there are also different lists of "trusted TSAs", so you need to keep your future audience in mind. For example, many of the TSAs which are in the eIDAS TSL are not built-in to the Windows CA/TSA store – and vice versa, many TSAs commonly trusted for Authenticode purposes won't be in the eIDAS TSL. (And alternative methods like Bitcoin "blockchain timestamping" are in neither.) Ultimately, no matter the method, you will have to convince the verifier that your chosen TSA (or blockchain or whatever) is indeed trusted for timestamping.

(Among other less-standard variants, there seems to be a long-running service providing PGP-based timestamps. A decade ago, before the big blockchain craze, there was a company named "Guardtime" specializing in timestamping services – once a month, instead of a CA certificate, they used to publish a Merkle Tree root hash in a newspaper as physical proof that all "leaf" hashes had existed before the paper was printed.)

1 Doesn't seem like they document it publicly though, but http://timestamp.apple.com/ts01 is what they use for "notarization" of macOS software.
